title: Hiring a SuiteScript Developer: What to Check First
excerpt: Before you hire a SuiteScript developer, know when custom scripts beat native NetSuite tools and how to vet code quality, testing, ownership and support.
content:
Your team has outgrown what NetSuite does out of the box. Maybe approvals still run through email, invoices need a calculation no saved search can handle, or someone exports data every morning so another system can use it. Eventually someone says you need a SuiteScript developer. They may be right. But the developer you choose matters more than the decision to customize. Good scripts quietly remove hours of manual work. Poor ones slow down record saves, break after a NetSuite release, and leave you holding code nobody else can read.

This guide is for owners, controllers and operations leaders who need to hire for SuiteScript work without becoming engineers themselves. It covers what the work involves, when you need it, and how to tell a careful developer from a risky one.

What a SuiteScript Developer Actually Does

SuiteScript is NetSuite's JavaScript-based platform for customizing the system beyond configuration. A SuiteScript developer writes code that runs inside your NetSuite account. In business terms, that code does one of a few jobs:

Business needTypical script typeWhat it looks like day to day
Enforce a rule or fill in data when a record is savedUser event scriptA sales order gets the right terms, territory or approval flag without anyone typing it
Guide users while they fill out a formClient scriptA warning appears before someone saves a vendor bill that doesn't match the PO
Process large batches on a scheduleScheduled or map/reduce scriptNightly updates to thousands of records, recurring billing prep, data cleanup
Build a custom screen or tool inside NetSuiteSuiteletAn approval queue, a bulk-edit screen or a purpose-built dashboard
Let another system send or pull dataRESTletYour CRM, e-commerce platform or warehouse system exchanging data with NetSuite
Add a step NetSuite workflows can't do nativelyWorkflow action scriptA visual approval workflow that calls custom logic at one step

You don't need to know how any of these are written. You do need to know that each one runs at a different moment and carries different risks. A slow user event script makes every save slower for every user. A poorly built scheduled script can fail partway through a batch and leave data half-updated. A good developer picks the right type for the job and explains why.

Do You Need SuiteScript at All?

Before hiring anyone, check whether native NetSuite tools already cover the need. Configuration is cheaper to build, easier for an admin to maintain and less likely to break during upgrades. Native options include:

  • Saved searches for reports, reminders and lists of records that need attention
  • SuiteFlow workflows for straightforward approvals and field updates
  • Custom fields, forms and records for capturing data your process needs
  • Formula fields for simple calculations that display on a record
  • Native imports and integrations for occasional data loads

SuiteScript is usually the right answer when one or more of these is true:

  • The logic has many conditions, lookups across records or math that workflows can't express cleanly
  • The volume is high enough that workflows run slowly or time out
  • You need a custom screen your team will use daily
  • Another system needs to exchange data with NetSuite reliably, not through manual exports
  • A workflow has grown so many branches that nobody can safely change it

A trustworthy developer will sometimes tell you that you don't need them. If every problem you describe gets the answer write a script, be cautious.

How to Vet a SuiteScript Developer

Resumes and certifications tell you someone has worked in NetSuite. They don't tell you whether the code will hold up in two years. These are the areas that separate durable work from fragile work.

They ask about the process before the code

The first conversation should be mostly questions. Who touches this record? What happens when the data is wrong? How many transactions run through it each month? What does the team do today when something fails? A developer who quotes a price before understanding the process is guessing, and the guess usually shows up later as rework.

They write in SuiteScript 2.x

SuiteScript 1.0 still runs, but the 2.x versions are the current standard and what NetSuite continues to invest in. New work should be in 2.x. If a developer proposes 1.0 for new scripts, ask why. There are rare reasons, but most of the time it signals outdated habits.

They respect governance limits

NetSuite limits how much work any script can do in a single run, measured in usage units. Scripts that ignore these limits work fine in testing with ten records and fail in production with ten thousand. Ask how they handle large volumes. A solid answer mentions map/reduce scripts, processing in batches and resuming cleanly after an interruption.

They build in a sandbox and deploy deliberately

Code should never be written directly in your live account. Ask where development and testing happen. A sandbox account is the usual answer. If you don't have one, a good developer will explain the tradeoffs and how they'll limit risk. Ask how changes move into production. Developers who use the SuiteCloud Development Framework (SDF) and keep code in version control can show exactly what changed and roll back if needed.

They plan for errors, not just success

Ask what happens when a script fails. Will anyone know? Good scripts log errors in a way your team can see, send alerts for failures that need action, and avoid leaving records in a half-updated state. Silent failure is one of the most expensive problems in custom NetSuite work because it surfaces weeks later as bad data.

They document and hand over ownership

You should own the code, have access to it outside NetSuite, and receive plain-English documentation of what each script does, when it runs and what it depends on. If your developer disappeared tomorrow, another competent SuiteScript developer should be able to pick up the work in days, not weeks.

They think about NetSuite releases

NetSuite ships two major releases a year. Most well-written scripts pass through untouched, but scripts that rely on unsupported tricks, such as manipulating page elements directly, can break. Ask how they test against upcoming releases and whether that's included in support.

Questions to Ask Before You Sign

Use these in your first or second conversation. You don't need to judge the technical detail of every answer. Listen for whether the answers are specific and calm or vague and defensive.

  1. What would you check before deciding this needs a script instead of a workflow?
  2. Which script type would you use here, and why?
  3. How will this perform when our transaction volume doubles?
  4. Where will you build and test it, and how does it get to production?
  5. What happens, and who finds out, if the script fails at 2 a.m.?
  6. What documentation will we receive, and where will the code live?
  7. Who supports this after launch, and how fast do you respond?
  8. How do you handle NetSuite's twice-yearly releases?

Freelancer, In-House Hire or Partner?

There's no single right model. The best choice depends on how much custom work you expect and how much risk you can absorb if a person becomes unavailable.

OptionWorks well whenWatch out for
Freelance SuiteScript developerYou have a small, well-defined project and someone internal can manage itSingle point of failure, inconsistent availability, support after launch
In-house developerYou have a steady pipeline of NetSuite work for years, not monthsFull-time cost, retention, nobody reviewing their code
Implementation or automation partnerThe work spans NetSuite plus other systems, or you want ongoing support without a hirePartners that push large projects when a small fix would do

Many mid-sized companies land on a mix: an internal NetSuite admin who handles configuration, plus an outside team for scripts and integrations. That keeps day-to-day changes in-house while giving complex work a second set of eyes.

Red Flags to Take Seriously

  • No questions about volume. Performance problems are the most common reason custom scripts get rewritten.
  • Building directly in production. Convenient for the developer, risky for your books.
  • No written scope. If the deliverable isn't defined, neither is done.
  • Reluctance to share code or documentation. You're paying for it. You should own it.
  • Everything is custom. Replacing native features with scripts creates maintenance you didn't need.
  • No plan for support. Scripts touch live data. Something will eventually need attention.

What a Good SuiteScript Engagement Looks Like

Whoever you hire, the work should follow a predictable path:

  1. Discovery. Map the current process, the records involved, volumes and failure points.
  2. Written scope. What the script will do, what it won't, and how success is measured, such as hours saved per week or errors eliminated.
  3. Build and test in a sandbox. Including edge cases: missing data, duplicate records, large batches.
  4. User acceptance testing. The people who use the process confirm it works the way they actually work.
  5. Controlled deployment. Scheduled for a low-risk window, with a rollback plan.
  6. Monitoring after launch. Someone watches logs and results closely for the first few weeks.

As a rough guide, a focused script or small automation can typically go live in a few weeks, while work that involves integrations with other systems takes longer. At Intellismart Group, most automations go live in 2 to 4 weeks and complex integrations take 6 to 8, and that's a reasonable benchmark to hold any SuiteScript developer to. If a quote is far shorter, ask what's been left out, usually testing or error handling.

Making the Decision

Hiring a SuiteScript developer is worth it when native NetSuite tools genuinely can't do the job and the payoff is clear in hours saved, errors avoided or software you no longer need to pay for. Start by confirming configuration won't solve the problem. Then judge candidates on how they handle the unglamorous parts: volume, testing, error handling, documentation and support. The developer who asks the most questions up front is usually the one whose scripts you'll never have to think about again.
topic: How business leaders decide whether they need a SuiteScript developer, and how to vet one so custom NetSuite scripts stay reliable, documented and supportable
